gotcha_text: Landlords leverage relocation clauses to move dental practices to inferior spaces to accommodate larger anchor tenants. This maneuver often leaves the tenant responsible for the massive capital expenditures required to replicate specialized clinical infrastructure.

deep_dive_html:
The Perils of Clinical Infrastructure Disruption

For dental practitioners, a lease is not merely a right to occupy space; it is a commitment to a highly specialized, capital-intensive environment. Relocation clauses, often buried in the 'Miscellaneous' or 'Subdivision' sections of a commercial lease, grant landlords the unilateral power to move your practice to a different suite within the building. While landlords argue this is necessary for building optimization, the technical reality for a dental office is far more sinister.

The primary danger lies in the 'cost-neutral' fallacy. Many standard-form leases stipulate that the landlord will pay for 'reasonable' costs associated with the move. In the context of a dental practice, 'reasonable' is a dangerously subjective term. A landlord may cover the cost of moving chairs, but they will likely attempt to avoid the massive expenses associated with re-installing specialized plumbing, compressed air lines, vacuum systems, and lead-integrated X-ray shielding.

The Standard for Tenant Protection

To mitigate this risk, a dental tenant must move beyond simple cost reimbursement and demand a comprehensive 'Make-Good' provision. An elite-level negotiation should focus on the following pillars:

  • Full Reimbursement of Specialized Build-Out: The clause must explicitly state that the landlord will pay for all costs to replicate the existing clinical configuration, including all mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) upgrades.
  • Business Interruption Indemnity: The lease must account for lost revenue during the downtime required for the relocation and subsequent permitting processes.
  • Right of Refusal: The tenant must have the right to inspect and reject the proposed new space if it does not meet the specific ergonomic or regulatory requirements of a dental clinic.
  • Permitting and Compliance: The landlord must be responsible for all costs related to obtaining new certificates of occupancy and ensuring the new space meets all healthcare-specific building codes.

title: Hidden Traps in Relocation Clauses for Dental Offices
